blocks.text: 1. overview

blocks.alt: An original dataset produces bootstrap samples that train many models

blocks.text: Random Forest and Extra Trees, covered in depth in the Classification module, both relied on bootstrap sampling and averaging or voting across many trees, but those mechanics were introduced there specifically as tree-based techniques, tightly bundled together with decision tree splitting rules and feature randomness. This Ensemble Learning module steps back to examine the actual general principle underneath both of them in its own right: Bagging, a technique that works with any base learner at all, not just decision trees.

Understanding Bagging as a standalone, general-purpose principle, separate from the specific tree-based machinery it happened to be introduced alongside, makes it possible to recognize the same underlying idea wherever it shows up, and to apply it deliberately to other kinds of models when the situation genuinely calls for it.
2. The General Bagging Procedure

blocks.alt: Sampling with replacement trains a model, and results get aggregated

blocks.text: Bagging, short for Bootstrap Aggregating, follows a simple three-step procedure that applies to any base learning algorithm. First, draw many separate bootstrap samples from the original training data, each one built by sampling rows with replacement, so each bootstrap sample is the same size as the original dataset but contains a different random mix of repeated and omitted rows, exactly the resampling process already covered in depth for Random Forest.

Second, train one entirely independent copy of the chosen base model on each of these bootstrap samples, producing many separately trained models, each having seen a slightly different version of the training data. Third, combine every one of these independently trained models' predictions into one final prediction, using a majority vote for classification tasks or a simple average for regression tasks. This three-step recipe, resample, train independently, combine, works identically regardless of what specific base learning algorithm is chosen for step two, decision trees, K-Nearest Neighbors, or even Logistic Regression.
3. Why Decision Trees Became the Usual Choice

Given that bagging works with any base learner in principle, it is worth asking directly why decision trees became by far the most common practical choice, to the point that many people first learn bagging exclusively through Random Forest. The answer lies in exactly which kinds of base learners actually benefit the most from bagging's variance-reduction effect, covered in more mathematical depth in the next section.

Decision trees, particularly when grown fairly deep, have a very specific statistical profile: naturally low bias, since a deep tree can fit almost any pattern in the training data, but very high variance, since small changes in the training data can produce a substantially different tree structure, exactly the tradeoff already covered in the Decision Trees topic. This is precisely the profile bagging is built to exploit and improve. A model that is already stable and low-variance on its own, such as plain Logistic Regression, has comparatively little to gain from bagging's variance-reduction effect, since there is not much variance left to reduce in the first place.
4. The Statistical Mechanism: Variance Reduction

blocks.alt: Bagging turns a high variance model into one with lower variance

blocks.text: The precise reason bagging works traces back directly to the bias-variance tradeoff, first framed in this course back in the Ridge Regression topic. A single high-variance base model, trained on just one particular sample of training data, produces predictions that would look noticeably different if trained on a slightly different sample instead, an instability that directly hurts how well it generalizes to genuinely new data.

Bagging exploits a basic statistical fact: averaging together many independently trained, only weakly correlated estimates of the same underlying quantity reduces the overall variance of that average substantially, while leaving the average's bias essentially unchanged from what any single one of those models would have had. This is exactly the mechanism already explained in mathematical depth for Random Forest's own variance-reduction behavior; the only difference here is recognizing that this same mechanism applies to averaging any independently trained high-variance models together, not specifically decision trees.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The variance-reduction benefit from averaging depends heavily on how correlated the individual bootstrap-trained models actually are with each other. Perfectly correlated models, ones that would make identical predictions regardless of which bootstrap sample they saw, gain nothing at all from averaging, which is exactly why Random Forest adds the extra feature-randomness layer covered in its own topic, to push correlation down even further than bootstrap sampling alone achieves.

blocks.text: 5. Out-of-Bag Evaluation, Generalized

blocks.alt: Out-of-bag points give a free evaluation estimate

blocks.text: Out-of-Bag evaluation, covered in depth as a feature of Random Forest specifically, is actually a general property of the bagging procedure itself, with nothing tree-specific about it at all. Because every bootstrap sample is built by sampling with replacement, roughly one third of the original training rows, on average, get left out of any given bootstrap sample entirely, regardless of what base learner is being trained on that sample.

This means any bagged ensemble, built from any base learner at all, can use exactly the same Out-of-Bag trick already covered for Random Forest: estimate each training row's prediction using only the models that never actually saw that row during their own training, providing a free validation estimate without needing to set aside a separate holdout split at all. This generalization is a direct, concrete illustration of why understanding bagging as a standalone principle matters, the exact same useful property applies just as well to a bagged ensemble of KNN models as it does to Random Forest's bagged decision trees.
6. Bagging Applied to Other Base Learners

blocks.alt: Bagging applies to decision trees and other base learners too

blocks.text: Seeing bagging applied to a base learner other than decision trees makes the general principle concrete. Bagged KNN builds many bootstrap samples, fits a separate KNN model to each one, and combines their predictions through voting or averaging, directly reducing KNN's sensitivity to exactly which specific training points happen to be nearest to a given query point, since different bootstrap samples will naturally include or exclude different specific neighbors.

It is also worth explicitly noting that bagged decision trees, without Random Forest's additional feature-randomness layer, are themselves a legitimate, useful bagging application on their own, one step short of the full Random Forest recipe. This version, sometimes just called Bagged Trees or Bagging Classifier in library implementations, still captures much of the variance-reduction benefit through bootstrap resampling alone, even without the extra decorrelation Random Forest's feature randomness provides on top.
7. Bagging versus Boosting

blocks.alt: Bagging trains models in parallel while boosting trains them sequentially

blocks.text: It is worth previewing the key contrast with Boosting, the very next topic in this module, since the two represent the two dominant families of ensemble methods and are frequently confused despite working in fundamentally different ways. Bagging trains many models independently and in parallel, each on its own separate bootstrap sample, with no model depending on any other model's output at all, and it primarily works by reducing variance.

Boosting instead trains many models sequentially, with each new model specifically targeting the errors still being made by the ensemble built so far, exactly the mechanism already covered for AdaBoost and Gradient Boosting in the Classification module, and it primarily works by reducing bias rather than variance. This difference in mechanism translates directly into a difference in overfitting behavior: bagging is naturally resistant to overfitting as more models are added to the ensemble, since averaging more independent estimates essentially never hurts, while boosting can genuinely overfit if left unchecked, since each new model is actively, aggressively chasing whatever error remains, including noise.

blocks.text: 8. When Bagging Genuinely Helps

blocks.alt: A high variance model is exactly where bagging helps

blocks.text: Bagging delivers the largest, most reliable benefit when the chosen base learner naturally has low bias but high variance, deep decision trees being the textbook example already covered throughout the Classification module. In this situation, bagging directly attacks the base learner's main weakness, variance, while leaving its main strength, low bias, essentially untouched.

When the base learner already has low variance on its own, a simple, heavily regularized linear model for instance, bagging has comparatively little left to improve, and the extra computational cost of training many separate copies of that model may not be worth the modest gain. Bagging also tends to help more when the training data itself is noisy or limited in size, since averaging predictions across many different bootstrap samples helps smooth out the effect of that noise, producing a more stable, reliable final prediction than any single model trained on the full, noisy dataset alone would achieve.

blocks.text: 9. Worked Example
The example below applies bagging to two very different base learners, decision trees and KNN, comparing each bagged ensemble against its single, unbagged counterpart.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = np.vstack([
    rng.normal(loc=[0, 0], scale=2, size=(100, 2)),
    rng.normal(loc=[6, 6], scale=2, size=(100, 2)),
])
y = np.array([0] * 100 + [1] * 100)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)

base_learners = {
    "Decision Tree (deep, high variance)": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=None, random_state=42),
    "KNN (k=1, high variance)": KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=1),
}

for name, base_model in base_learners.items():
    single_scores = cross_val_score(base_model, X_train, y_train, cv=5)
    bagged_model = BaggingClassifier(estimator=base_model, n_estimators=50, random_state=42)
    bagged_scores = cross_val_score(bagged_model, X_train, y_train, cv=5)
    print(f"{name}:")
    print(f"  Single model CV accuracy: {single_scores.mean():.3f} (+/- {single_scores.std():.3f})")
    print(f"  Bagged ensemble CV accuracy: {bagged_scores.mean():.3f} (+/- {bagged_scores.std():.3f})")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Watch the standard deviation, not just the mean accuracy, across cross-validation folds. Bagging typically reduces that standard deviation noticeably for both base learners, a direct, measurable demonstration of the variance-reduction effect covered throughout this topic.

blocks.text: 10. Key Takeaways

items: Bagging is the general principle underneath Random Forest and Extra Trees: resample with bootstrapping, train independently, combine by voting or averaging.
It applies to any base learner, not just decision trees, though decision trees became the most common practical choice.
Bagging helps most with base learners that are naturally low-bias but high-variance, exactly the profile deep decision trees have.
It works by averaging many independently trained, weakly correlated models, reducing variance while leaving bias roughly unchanged.
Out-of-Bag evaluation is a general property of bagging itself, usable with any base learner, not just decision trees.
Bagged KNN and bagged decision trees without extra feature randomness both illustrate bagging applied beyond Random Forest specifically.
Bagging trains models independently and in parallel; Boosting, covered next, trains models sequentially instead.
Bagging primarily reduces variance and resists overfitting as more models are added; Boosting primarily reduces bias.
Next up: Boosting, examined here as its own general principle, the sequential error-correction idea behind AdaBoost and Gradient Boosting.
